title: Manage equine ration formulation and feeding

lessons.title: The equine digestive tract
lessons.html:
A trickle-feeding hindgut fermenter

The horse evolved to graze for most of the day on fibrous forage, eating small amounts almost continuously. Its digestive tract is designed for that, and most feeding-related disease in stabled horses comes from management that ignores it. A feeding manager must understand each section and what it does.

SectionFeaturesManagement implication
Mouth and teethLips select feed; molars grind fibre; chewing produces saliva that buffers stomach acidDental problems reduce chewing efficiency and cause weight loss and choke; forage promotes chewing and saliva
OesophagusOne-way valve into the stomach; horses effectively cannot vomitDry, bolted feed (especially pellets or beet pulp not soaked) can cause choke; toxins cannot be expelled
StomachSmall relative to body size; acid is secreted continuously; upper (non-glandular) area poorly protectedLarge meals overflow quickly; long periods without forage increase gastric ulcer risk
Small intestineMain site of enzymatic digestion of starch, sugar, protein and fat; absorption of most vitamins and mineralsStarch capacity is limited; large grain meals overflow undigested into the hindgut
CaecumLarge fermentation vat; microbes digest fibreSudden diet changes disturb the microbes
Large colonMain site of microbial fermentation, producing volatile fatty acids for energy; absorbs water; has several bends (flexures)Flexures are common sites of impaction colic; adequate water and forage are essential
Small colon and rectumWater absorption and formation of droppingsDry, hard droppings indicate inadequate water or fibre

The hindgut microbes

Bacteria and protozoa in the caecum and colon break down fibre that the horse's own enzymes cannot. They are sensitive to change. When large amounts of starch reach the hindgut, starch-fermenting bacteria multiply, lactic acid accumulates, the gut becomes acidic and fibre-digesting microbes die. Toxins released can trigger colic and laminitis. This is why grain overload is an emergency.

Consequences for feeding

  • Forage should be the base of every ration.
  • Concentrates should be fed in several small meals rather than one or two large ones.
  • All changes in feed type should be gradual.
  • Clean water must always be available.
  • Horses should not go long periods without access to forage.

lessons.title: Principles of ration formulation
lessons.html:
Nutrients the ration must supply

NutrientMain sourcesNotes
WaterTroughs, buckets, moisture in grassThe most important nutrient; needs rise sharply with heat, sweating and lactation
EnergyFibre (via fermentation), starch, sugar, oilUsually expressed as digestible energy (DE) in megajoules (MJ)
ProteinLucerne, soya, sunflower oilcakeQuality depends on essential amino acids, especially lysine
MineralsForage, concentrates, licks, supplementsCalcium and phosphorus ratio is critical; also salt, magnesium, trace elements such as copper, zinc and selenium
VitaminsFresh grazing, good hay, supplementsStored hay loses vitamins A and E over time

Steps in formulating a ration

  1. Estimate body weight with a weighbridge or a weight tape and formula.
  2. Assess body condition using a condition scoring system (for example a 1-9 scale) and decide whether to maintain, gain or lose weight.
  3. Define the workload and life stage: maintenance, light, moderate, heavy or intense work; growth; late pregnancy; lactation; old age.
  4. Calculate daily requirements for energy, protein, calcium, phosphorus and other nutrients from recognised feeding standards (for example NRC tables) or software.
  5. Estimate total feed intake. A commonly used guideline is total daily dry matter intake of roughly 2 to 2.5% of body weight, with forage making up the majority. Treat this as a starting point, not a fixed rule.
  6. Choose and analyse forage. Forage varies widely. A laboratory analysis of hay (for example eragrostis, teff or lucerne) gives its energy, protein and mineral content.
  7. Calculate what forage supplies and identify the shortfall.
  8. Fill the gap with concentrate, a balancer or supplements, keeping concentrate to the minimum needed.
  9. Check the mineral balance, especially the calcium to phosphorus ratio. Calcium should not fall below phosphorus; grain-heavy rations are often high in phosphorus.
  10. Cost the ration in rand per horse per day and look for efficiencies.

Feed in weight, not volume

A scoop of oats and a scoop of pellets weigh different amounts. A ration is formulated in kilograms, so every feed must be weighed at least once to calibrate the scoops, and hay nets weighed regularly. Feed labels on registered commercial feeds show guaranteed analysis; under Act 36 of 1947 farm feeds sold in South Africa must be registered.

Using expertise

Commercial feed companies and equine nutritionists can formulate or check rations. The manager's role is to supply accurate information (weights, workload, forage analysis), interpret the advice, and monitor the result.

lessons.title: Individual rations and feeding management
lessons.html:
Every horse is an individual

Two horses of the same weight doing the same work can need very different rations because of temperament, metabolism, age and health. Group rations are a starting point; individual adjustment is the manager's job.

Examples of individual requirements

HorseRation emphasis
Racehorse in trainingHigh energy density; part of energy from oil to reduce starch load; electrolytes; split concentrate into several meals
Easy-keeping pony or cobRestricted, lower-energy forage; balancer instead of concentrate; grazing muzzle or restricted grazing; monitor for laminitis
Broodmare, late pregnancy and lactationIncreased energy, protein, calcium and phosphorus; good quality forage; balanced minerals for the foal
Growing youngstockCorrect protein quality and minerals; avoid excess energy and rapid growth that can contribute to developmental orthopaedic disease
Old horse with poor teethSoaked fibre feeds, chopped forage, soaked pellets; regular dental care
Horse with a history of ulcersConstant forage access, lucerne before exercise, low starch

The feed chart

Each horse should have a written feed chart on its stable door and in the feed room, showing the horse's name, each feed by weight, times of feeding, supplements and any medication. The chart is signed and dated when changed. Grooms must feed exactly to the chart.

Rules of feeding

  • Feed plenty of forage; keep periods without forage short.
  • Feed concentrate in small meals, ideally three or more per day for horses on high concentrate rations.
  • Feed at regular times.
  • Make all changes gradually, typically over one to two weeks.
  • Do not work a horse hard immediately after a large concentrate meal.
  • Use good quality, dust-free, mould-free feed; soak or steam dusty hay for horses with respiratory problems.
  • Keep feed stores secure and rodent-free; lock concentrate rooms so a loose horse cannot gorge.
  • Never feed cattle or poultry feeds to horses. Some contain ionophores such as monensin, which are highly toxic to horses even in small amounts.

Monitoring

Weigh or weight-tape horses every two to four weeks and condition score them. Record feed refusals, droppings, behaviour and performance. Adjust the ration in small steps and review again. Keep records of feed purchases and usage to control cost and detect wastage or theft.

lessons.title: Nutritional disorders, additives and supplements
lessons.html:
Managing nutritional disorders

DisorderNutritional causesPrevention and management
ColicSudden feed changes, grain overload, poor forage, too little water, sand ingestionRegular routine, gradual changes, water, good forage; call the vet immediately for signs of colic
LaminitisGrain overload, lush pasture high in sugars, obesity and insulin dysregulationControl body weight and sugar/starch intake, restrict grazing; veterinary emergency
Gastric ulcersLong periods without forage, high starch meals, stress of training and travelConstant forage, lower starch, lucerne; vet diagnosis by gastroscopy and treatment
ChokeBolting dry feed, dental problems, unsoaked beet pulpSoak feeds as instructed, spread feed out, dental care
Obesity / equine metabolic syndromeExcess energy for workloadWeighed, restricted forage; exercise; vet assessment
Exertional rhabdomyolysis (tying-up)High starch rations in susceptible horses, electrolyte imbalanceLower starch and higher oil; consistent exercise; vet-guided management
Nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism ("big head")Low calcium, high phosphorus rations, or grazing oxalate-rich grasses such as kikuyu and some setariaCorrect calcium supplementation and diet balance under veterinary advice
Developmental orthopaedic disease in youngstockImbalanced minerals, excess energy, rapid growthBalanced ration, controlled growth

The manager's responsibility is early recognition, immediate referral to the veterinarian when signs are acute, and correction of the underlying ration.

Feed additives and supplements

Additives and supplements are used to correct a known deficiency or support a specific need. Common categories:

  • Vitamin and mineral balancers - correct shortfalls in forage-based rations
  • Electrolytes - replace salts lost in sweat in hard-working horses
  • Oils - increase energy density without starch
  • Yeast and probiotics - aim to support hindgut function
  • Hoof supplements (for example biotin), joint and coat supplements

Managing their use

  1. Identify the need first, based on ration analysis, condition and veterinary advice.
  2. Avoid stacking several supplements that contain the same nutrients; some, such as selenium, are toxic in excess.
  3. Use registered products and follow the label for dose.
  4. For competition and racehorses, check every product against the racing or sport body's prohibited substances rules; some herbal and imported products contain banned substances.
  5. Record what each horse receives and evaluate whether the supplement produces the intended effect; stop those that do not.

Key points

  • The horse is a trickle-feeding hindgut fermenter with a small stomach that cannot vomit.
  • Formulate from body weight, condition, workload and forage analysis; forage first.
  • Feed by weight, in small regular meals, and change rations gradually.
  • Never feed ionophore-containing cattle or poultry feeds to horses.
  • Use supplements only for an identified need, at label doses, and check racing rules.
